entities.summary:
The People's Party (Partido Popular, PP) of Spain, founded in 1989 from the People's Alliance (founded 1976 by Manuel Fraga, a Franco-era minister), is Spain's principal center-right party and the Spanish affiliate of the European People's Party — alternating government with the Socialist Party (PSOE) in Spain's two-party system from 1996-2018. The PP's 1996-2004 government under José María Aznar committed Spain to the Iraq War despite 90% public opposition — one of the most extreme examples of democratic government acting against public opinion — and the 2004 Madrid bombings were timed three days before Spain's election, killing 191 people.

Manuel Fraga, a former Franco cabinet minister who unsuccessfully ran in Spain's first democratic elections (1977), founded the right-wing People's Alliance in 1976. The PP's 1996 victory brought José María Aznar to power as Spain's first right-wing post-Franco prime minister. Aznar's presidency included Spain's euro zone entry (1999), unprecedented economic growth (the 'Spanish Miracle'), and decisive support for the US-led Iraq War invasion — standing alongside Bush and Blair despite 90% Spanish public opposition.

The March 11, 2004 Madrid Bombings (191 killed, 1,800 injured) — Spain's deadliest terrorist attack — came three days before the general election. The Aznar government's initial insistence on attributing the attack to ETA (despite evidence pointing to Al-Qaeda), perceived as electoral manipulation, contributed to the PP's surprise election defeat. The PP has since alternated government with PSOE, returning to power under Mariano Rajoy (2011-2018) and Alberto Núñez Feijóo (2023-).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Spain's People's Party represents the successful democratic transformation of Francoism into European center-right governance — and Aznar's Iraq War commitment against 90% public opposition became a case study in democratic leaders overriding mass public opinion.
